about: What the owner's grades and voice notes taught, and what shipped games teach, as rules the words work reads before it writes or chooses a line (owner, Nov 9, 12:45 a.m.: "so that these shitty lines don't happen again"). A rule with features is also a lesson on the grade map (src/english/grade-map.ts): each feature takes the strength given on every line that holds it, in the rule context. A rule with no features is checked by the writer and the grounding reviewer, not by the map. Sources: the owner's quotes with their files, and docs/research/dialogue/2026-11-09-how-games-write-dialogue.md.

rules.rule: A line names something specific from its situation (a person, place, thing, amount or day), not a general sentiment.

sources.quote: I would like it if they said why.

rules.rule: A scene opens with narration naming the day, the place and the person: "First thing on June 7th. You head to the clerk's office and speak to Maria Patton."

sources.quote: If it's June 7th, it says first thing on June 7th. You head to the clerk's office and speak to Maria Patton. And then it starts like that.
sources.file: owner ruling, Nov 8 (CTO brief for the Nov 9 Story run)

rules.rule: A question names what it asks about; "What do you think?" alone fails.

sources.quote: What does that mean?

rules.rule: A line never points at "this", "that" or "it" when nothing in the line or the scene has named it.

sources.quote: Got a minute for Woem? Who is Woem?
What does that mean?

rules.rule: No filler: no "Well," "Look," "So," opening and no "you know" or "I mean" padding a line that has nothing else to say.

sources.quote: filler
sources.file: owner ruling, Nov 8, 2:22 p.m. (CTO brief): this is why it feels like i've seen the same dialogue for 2 weeks

rules.rule: No stock phrase a script reaches for when there is nothing to say ("moving forward", "at the end of the day", "I hear you").
No line explains its own subtext or tells the player what to feel.
No instant, agreeable wrap-up: a reply may push back, deflect or escalate instead of giving in in one line.

sources.quote: That sounds like AI. It's like, okay, quick resolution. That's not how normal people talk.

rules.rule: An evasion points to a later time or the public record, not a bare refusal.

sources.quote: I'll have something to say after the vote is most natural.

rules.rule: No election-insider, developer or office-chart words; say canvassing, campaign signs, the finance secretary.

sources.quote: Don't say gaps, though. That is dev language.

rules.rule: No narration of the form "You're in <place>" or "<person> is with you".

sources.quote: Remove every instance of that from the English engine.

rules.rule: A line that commits (a stance, a threat, a refusal) names who, what or why in plain words.

sources.quote: I would like it if they said why.

rules.rule: A plea gives its stake; a bargain names the trade; a complaint names the concrete effect.

sources.quote: A plea gives its stake

rules.rule: A reply answers or follows the line right before it.

sources.quote: And then the reply, I will, first thing on the agenda, in my own words. What?

rules.rule: Every person, outlet, office or thing is named to the player before a line addresses it.

sources.quote: Got a minute for Woem? Who is Woem?

rules.rule: A line speaks in the tense the record is in: no talking about a vote as done before it happens.

sources.quote: it's talking like it's in the present, but the vote hasn't happened yet.

rules.rule: A line fits its speaker's role, age and relationship to the listener, and a speaker is recognizable without the name attached.

sources.quote: you might say something to your mom that you would never say to a coworker

rules.rule: Threats and pressure sound like politics (memory, friends, how it works), never a generic warning.

sources.quote: I like that. I like that a lot.

rules.rule: A scene ends on a beat that lands, not a pleasantry, and never while a grievance or a count is still open.

sources.quote: But the conversation shouldn't really end after that.

rules.rule: When a request is made of the player, a clarifying "Why me?" reply exists and the other person answers it.

sources.quote: it can be an auto reply to keep the conversation going

rules.rule: No one shape repeats across scenes: vary who speaks first, how long, and where the narrator breaks in; a line said once is not said again by the same person soon.

sources.quote: It needs to be varied.

rules.rule: A speech is not a list of figures: it takes a stance, reads as speech, and fits the speaker and the moment.

sources.quote: it shouldn't read as a list. That's not how normal people talk.

rules.rule: Prefer wit or a concrete image over a generic statement when the voice allows it.

sources.quote: That scene was great

rules.rule: A trade or offer reads as a bribe only when it is one; build the trade from the district's interests.

sources.quote: it sounds like it's going to be a bribe, but it's not.

rules.rule: Variants of a slot differ in what they say, each tied to a fact in the record, not only in wording; a bank grows by adding conditions and specifics, not more generic lines.
The most specific matching line wins: a line tied to the speaker's trait and the situation outranks a generic one.
